Your AI systems may be brilliant. Are they auditable?

SOC 2 compliance was designed for a world where data moved predictably between defined systems with documented controls.

Generative AI broke that model — and most enterprise security teams haven't caught up.

The AICPA's Trust Services Criteria (TSC, updated 2022, CC6–CC9) define the control categories every SOC 2 Type II audit evaluates: logical access, change management, risk mitigation, monitoring. These criteria were written for deterministic systems — code that does the same thing every time, with outputs you can verify against inputs.

A large language model is not that system.

When a language model is part of your production stack, the TSC framework faces questions it was not architected to answer — and your auditors are beginning to ask them:

→ What is the "completeness and accuracy" control (CC7.2) for a system whose outputs are probabilistic by design?
→ How do you establish "change management" controls (CC8.1) for a model that updates through fine-tuning or prompt engineering?
→ What does "logical access control" (CC6.1) mean when your AI has retrieval access to internal knowledge bases?
→ How do you satisfy "monitoring" requirements (CC7.1) for outputs generated at scale and reviewed by exception?

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, January 2023, pp. 1–43) addresses this directly. Its four core functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — establish that trustworthiness properties must be measurable and documented, not asserted.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 goes further: mandatory AI impact assessments, documented oversight, AI policy governance. It is the ISO 27001 of AI — and enterprise procurement is beginning to require it.

Wachter, Mittelstadt & Russell, in Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box (Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, 2017, Vol. 31, No. 2, pp. 841–887), established the legal and technical framework: AI decisions must be reconstructable, contestable, and auditable. Enterprise contracts are now citing this standard.

The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, Articles 9–17) imposes binding requirements — risk management systems, technical documentation, logging, human oversight — on high-risk AI. SOC 2 alone does not satisfy them.

What SOC-compliant AI architecture actually requires:

1. Immutable audit logs (TSC CC7.2, NIST AI RMF Measure 2.5)
Every AI output logged with input, model version, timestamp, retrieval context. Non-negotiable in a Type II audit.

2. Access controls on RAG systems (CC6.1, ISO 42001 §6.1.2)
If your AI retrieves internal data, access control rigor must match any system with that data access.

3. Human-in-the-loop documentation (CC4.1, EU AI Act Art. 14)
Where AI runs without human review: document risk acceptance and monitoring compensating controls.

4. Model versioning & change management (CC8.1, NIST AI RMF Govern 1.4)
Prompt changes, fine-tuning events — these are production changes. Treat them as such.

5. Vendor risk management (CC9.2)
Your AI provider's security posture is your risk. Auditors will ask for the assessment.

I design enterprise AI applications with these controls built in from day one — not retrofitted under audit pressure.

The cost of building compliance in is a fraction of the cost of losing an enterprise deal because your security team can't answer a procurement questionnaire.

─────────────────────────────
References:
¹ AICPA. Trust Services Criteria (2022). CC6–CC9.
² NIST. AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (January 2023). pp. 1–43.
³ ISO/IEC 42001:2023. AI Management System Standard.
⁴ Wachter, S., Mittelstadt, B. & Russell, C. (2017). Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box. Harvard Journal of Law & Technology. Vol. 31, No. 2, pp. 841–887.
⁵ EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 9–17.
─────────────────────────────

The tech industry is eating itself alive.

52% of the internet is now AI-generated content. (Graphite, 2025)
"Slop" — AI-generated junk — was Merriam-Webster's Word of the Year 2025.
78% of AI startups are literally just API wrappers. (CB Insights, 2024)

We built the most powerful creative tools in history.
Then immediately used them to flood the world with garbage.

Here's the full breakdown — and why this ends badly for everyone building right now 🧵

Let's talk about the piracy problem nobody wants to say out loud.

Meta downloaded 81 terabytes of books from Anna's Archive — a pirated library — to train their models. NVIDIA contacted Anna's Archive directly to access 500TB of pirated data for NeMo and InstructRetro. This came out in unsealed court documents.

Getty Images is suing Stability AI for $1.7 billion.
The RIAA sued Suno and Udio for $150,000 per infringed work.
The New York Times is suing OpenAI.

In 2023, Ghostwriter977 dropped a Drake deepfake — "Heart on My Sleeve" — using AI-cloned vocals. 9M TikTok shares. 250K Spotify streams. Pulled by Universal Music Group two weeks later.

The boring truth: the AI content boom was built on unlicensed work. The legal bills are arriving.

We didn't invent new creativity. We laundered someone else's.

Now add the pseudo-creativity layer.

95% of generative AI pilots in enterprise delivered zero measurable financial return. (MIT NANDA report, July 2025 — 300 deployments analyzed)

42% of enterprise AI projects were abandoned in 2025 — up from 17% the year before. (S&P Global, 1,006 companies surveyed)

Why?

Because most of them are adding unnecessary flavor instead of solving real problems.

AI-generated thumbnails that look slightly off. AI-written emails that sound like AI. AI customer service bots that gaslight users and escalate tickets. AI "summaries" that miss the entire point of the document.

We took genuine capability — LLMs that can reason, generate, retrieve — and used it to produce content that satisfies a checklist instead of a human.

Capability without judgment isn't innovation. It's noise at scale.

Here's where the corporate law angle gets ugly.

California SB 1047 would have required AI safety testing before deployment. Big Tech spent millions lobbying. Newsom vetoed it in September 2024.

Patent troll activity grew 15–20% in 2025 vs. 2024. (Unified Patents) Shell companies filing broad AI patents — not to build anything, just to extract licensing fees from companies that actually are building.

WordPress rejected 86% of DMCA notices in H2 2025 — defective, automated, or AI-generated. Small creators without legal teams can't fight back the same way.

The pattern: companies with one overwhelming strength — lawyers, lobbyists, or capital — are using that single card to lock in the whole game.

They didn't win by building better. They won by making it expensive for everyone else to build at all.

That's not competition. That's capture.

So what do you actually do with this if you're building?

1. Don't build on stolen foundations. Use licensed training data or open-weight models with clean provenance (Llama, Mistral). The lawsuits will eventually catch up — and they'll find the companies underneath too.

2. Reject pseudo-creativity. If your AI feature saves someone 0 minutes per week, kill it. If users immediately re-edit the output, kill it. Ship things that work for real humans.

3. Watch the regulatory capture playbook. The companies blocking safety legislation aren't doing it because regulation is bad. They're doing it because compliance costs are a moat — and they can afford it, you can't.

4. Build moats that can't be lobbied away. Proprietary data. Real user relationships. Evaluations the big players can't replicate.

The tech that survives this phase isn't the most viral. It's the most defensible.

Follow for more on building AI systems that actually ship.

The First Amendment doesn't protect your right to be heard. It protects the government's inability to silence you. That's a very different thing.

The First Amendment states: "Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press."

Note the operative subject: Congress.

Isaiah Berlin, in Two Concepts of Liberty (Oxford, 1958, pp. 7–16), drew the defining distinction: negative liberty is freedom from coercive interference. Positive liberty is the actual capacity to act. The First Amendment is a masterwork of negative liberty. It was never designed to guarantee positive liberty — the capacity to speak, be heard, and participate in public discourse.

The First Amendment says nothing about:

→ A platform's right to remove or suppress your content
→ A corporation's right to decline to publish your story
→ An algorithm's right to deprioritize your reach below public visibility
→ An advertiser's right to withdraw funding when journalism becomes inconvenient

Tim Wu, in The Master Switch (Knopf, 2010, pp. 6–12), documents the recurring pattern he calls "the Cycle" — every major communications technology begins open, then consolidates under private control. Radio. Film. Cable television. The internet is not an exception. It is the latest iteration.

Yochai Benkler argued in The Wealth of Networks (Yale, 2006, pp. 1–28) that decentralised internet architecture could democratise the public sphere. That argument was correct in 2006. It is less correct after two decades of platform consolidation rebuilt gatekeeping at the infrastructure layer.

The relevant law:

Section 230 (47 U.S.C. § 230, 1996) — platform immunity from third-party content liability — has not been substantively amended in 28 years.

The EU Digital Services Act (Regulation 2022/2065) — requiring algorithmic transparency audits and systemic risk assessments — is the most rigorous platform governance framework in force. The U.S. has no equivalent.

Zeynep Tufekci, in Twitter and Tear Gas (Yale, 2017, pp. 237–266), identifies "algorithmic gatekeeping" — the capacity of platform architecture to shape which political realities become legible to public audiences. Censorship without a censor. Structural, invisible, constitutionally unaddressed.

The regulatory gap between where technology operates and where law reaches is one of the most significant accountability vacuums in contemporary governance.

Free media requires positive liberty — economic viability, distribution access, algorithmic transparency — without which the formal right to speak is functionally meaningless.

Those conditions do not currently exist at scale.

─────────────────────────────
References:
¹ Berlin, I. (1958). Two Concepts of Liberty. Oxford. pp. 7–16.
² Wu, T. (2010). The Master Switch. Knopf. pp. 6–12.
³ Benkler, Y. (2006). The Wealth of Networks. Yale. pp. 1–28.
⁴ Tufekci, Z. (2017). Twitter and Tear Gas. Yale. pp. 237–266.
⁵ 47 U.S.C. § 230 (1996). ⁶ EU DSA Regulation 2022/2065.
─────────────────────────────

POST 1/5:

Side projects don't get you hired.

Tutorial projects with a fresh coat of paint don't either.

I reviewed 200+ junior resumes last year. 90% had the same 3 projects: a to-do app, a weather API, a Netflix clone.

Zero callbacks. Zero interviews. Zero offers.

Here's what I learned 🧵

---

POST 2/5:

The boring truth: recruiters don't care about your tech stack.

They care about one thing — did you solve a problem someone actually has?

A to-do app solves nothing. There are 10,000 to-do apps.

A Netflix clone proves you can follow a YouTube tutorial. That's not engineering. That's transcription.

I built NoshSource in 2020. It hit 5,000 daily users.

Not because the code was elegant. Because hungry people in my city needed cheap food during COVID, and I gave it to them.

That one project got me more interviews than my entire GitHub combined.

---

POST 3/5:

The turning point for me was realizing this:

Engineers who get hired build things that have users.

Not stars on GitHub. Users. Real humans who open the app twice a week.

Once I understood that, my project filter changed completely.

Before: "What's a cool tech stack to learn?"
After: "What's a problem 100 people would pay $5/month to solve?"

The second question is harder. That's the point.

Most juniors skip it because it's uncomfortable. They'd rather rebuild Twitter for the 4,000th time.

---

POST 4/5:

If I were starting today, I'd build projects using this framework:

1. Pick a niche you already live in (gym, college, gaming, faith community, immigrant community).

2. Find 10 people in that niche. Ask what wastes their time weekly.

3. Build the ugliest possible v1 in 2 weeks. Ship it.

4. Get 50 real users. Not friends. Strangers.

5. Add ONE AI feature that actually helps (RAG over their data, automated workflows, smart search). Not a ChatGPT wrapper.

6. Write a case study: problem → users → metrics → tech decisions.

7. Put the case study at the top of your resume. Not the bottom.

This beats 4 tutorial projects every single time.

---

POST 5/5:

Recap:

→ Tutorial projects signal that you can follow instructions.
→ User-facing projects signal that you can think.
→ Recruiters skim for signals. Give them the right one.

Build 1 project with 50 real users instead of 5 projects with 0.

I spent 4 years learning this the hard way so you don't have to.

Most people think they have access to a free press. They don't.

The illusion of media pluralism is one of the most consequential blind spots in modern democratic life — and it has a theoretical name.

Jürgen Habermas, in The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962; MIT Press, 1989, pp. 181–195), argued that a functioning democracy requires a communicative space where citizens engage in rational-critical discourse, free from commercial and state distortion. He called it the Öffentlichkeit — the public sphere. His central thesis: when that sphere is colonised by market forces, democratic legitimacy erodes at the root.

We are living that thesis in real time.

Six corporations — Comcast, Disney, News Corp, Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, and Fox — control approximately 90% of what Americans read, watch, and hear. Ben Bagdikian documented this trajectory across seven editions of The Media Monopoly (Beacon Press, 1983–2004). In 1983, fifty companies dominated U.S. media. By the 2004 edition (The New Media Monopoly, pp. 1–27), that number had collapsed to five.

Herman and Chomsky's Propaganda Model, introduced in Manufacturing Consent (Pantheon, 1988, Ch. 1, pp. 1–35), identifies five systemic filters: ownership, advertising dependency, sourcing, disciplinary flak, and dominant ideology. These filters don't require editorial orders. They operate structurally — through incentive design. Stories that threaten advertiser relationships or ownership investments are not killed. They are never commissioned.

Nicholas Garnham, in Capitalism and Communication (Sage, 1990, pp. 1–19), frames the core contradiction: information, as a public good, increases in value with distribution. But the market treats it as a commodity whose value depends on scarcity. You cannot simultaneously maximise the social utility of information and the private profit from it.

Isaiah Berlin's distinction between negative liberty (freedom from interference) and positive liberty (the actual capacity to act) is instructive — Two Concepts of Liberty (1958). The First Amendment secures negative press freedom admirably. It says nothing about the positive conditions — economic viability, distribution access — without which press freedom is a legal abstraction with no operational reality.

Pew Research Center documents U.S. newsroom employment falling 26% between 2008 and 2020. Northwestern University's Local News Initiative identified 200+ counties — home to over 200 million Americans — as news deserts with no dedicated local coverage (The State of Local News, 2022, p. 4).

The infrastructure of democratic accountability is not failing because of malice. It is failing because we built a media economy optimised for engagement and scale rather than truth and civic function.

That is a systems design problem. Systems design problems have systems design solutions.

What those look like — next post.

─────────────────────────────

¹ Habermas (1989) The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere. MIT Press. pp. 181–195.
² Bagdikian (2004) The New Media Monopoly. Beacon Press. pp. 1–27.
³ Herman & Chomsky (1988) Manufacturing Consent. Pantheon. Ch. 1, pp. 1–35.
